title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption

severity.usersAffected: Thousands of websites and services worldwide dependent on S3 US-EAST-1
severity.impactUsd: ≈ US$150M+ estimated loss to S&P-500 companies (Cyence, via press)
servicesDown: AWS Service Health Dashboard (couldn't update — hosted on S3)

brief: An authorized S3 engineer running an established capacity-removal playbook mistyped one input; the command removed far more servers than intended, taking down the S3 index and placement subsystems in US-EAST-1. Because a very large number of services (and AWS's own status dashboard) depend on S3, the ~4.5-hour disruption cascaded across a large fraction of the internet.

magnitude.note: Blast radius extreme: S3 is a foundational dependency for a large share of the public internet; cascade reached EC2/EBS/Lambda and even AWS's own status page.

sequenceOfEvents.event: Authorized S3 team member executes an established playbook command to remove a small number of billing-subsystem servers; one input is entered incorrectly, removing a larger server set than intended.
The removed capacity forces a full restart of the S3 index subsystem (tracks metadata/location of all US-EAST-1 objects) and the placement subsystem (allocates new storage).
S3 GET/LIST/PUT/DELETE/POST APIs return errors region-wide; dependent AWS services (EC2 launches, EBS, Lambda) and countless third-party sites degrade or fail.
AWS Service Health Dashboard cannot show red status because its own tooling depends on S3 US-EAST-1; AWS communicates via the dashboard banner and Twitter instead.
Index subsystem recovery reported as progressing; S3 begins returning to normal for retrieval operations.
S3 PUT/DELETE/POST (write) operations fully recovered; region operating normally.

rootCause: Human input error during a routine, authorized capacity-removal operation: a typo in one command argument removed a much larger set of servers than intended. The affected servers supported two S3 subsystems (index and placement) that then required a full restart. These subsystems had not been completely restarted for many years and had grown large, so the safety checks, metadata re-validation, and restart took far longer than expected — turning a capacity change into a multi-hour regional outage.
contributingFactors: Capacity-removal tooling allowed removing too much capacity too quickly, with no floor on minimum required capacity for a subsystem.
Index and placement subsystems had not been fully restarted in years and had scaled up substantially, making cold restart slow and risky.
Broad, hidden dependency of many AWS services on S3 in a single region turned a storage fault into a wide cascade.
The AWS Service Health Dashboard's own control plane depended on S3 US-EAST-1, so status could not be updated during the event.

coe.action: Modify the capacity-removal tool to remove capacity more slowly and to prevent it from taking any subsystem below its minimum required capacity level.
Audit other operational tools for the same class of fast/unsafe capacity actions and add equivalent safety guards.
Partition the S3 index subsystem into smaller cells so recovery is faster and blast radius is smaller; improve restart time of index/placement subsystems.
Change the AWS Service Health Dashboard to run across multiple regions so it can report status even when one region is impaired.

lessonsLearnt: Routine, well-practised operational commands are still high-consequence: guard destructive/scaling actions with rate limits and hard minimum-capacity floors, not just runbooks.
Subsystems that are never restarted accumulate hidden restart risk; exercise cold-start/recovery paths deliberately so real recovery time is known.
Single-region dependency concentration converts a component fault into a systemic one; understand and reduce cross-service blast radius.
Status/observability control planes must not depend on the very system whose health they report.
improvements: Rate-limited capacity operations with enforced minimum-capacity guardrails on the S3 tooling.
Cellularization of the S3 index subsystem to shrink blast radius and speed recovery.
Multi-region AWS Service Health Dashboard so status reporting survives a regional impairment.
Broader operational-tool audit for unsafe fast-acting capacity actions.
technicalDeepDive: S3 in a region is composed of many subsystems; two are central here. The index subsystem holds the metadata and physical location of every object in the region and is consulted on every GET/LIST/HEAD request — if it is unavailable, reads fail even though the underlying data is intact. The placement subsystem allocates storage for new objects and is required for PUT; it also depends on the index subsystem. Removing a large tranche of capacity forced both into a full restart. Because these subsystems had scaled to a very large footprint and had not been restarted for years, the restart had to perform extensive integrity checks and metadata reconciliation before serving traffic, which dominated the ~4.5-hour recovery. The event is a canonical example of AWS's own Correction-of-Errors (COE) culture and Sequence-of-Events (SOE) postmortem discipline: a precise timeline, an honest single-sentence root cause (operator input error on a scaling command), and concrete, verifiable remediations (guardrails, cellularization, multi-region status).
